drills.title: vs bbaldy87 (319) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black wants to trade off your attacking bishop on g5 with ...Bxg5, then swing the rook to g8 to harass whatever recaptures there. Re1 ignored that completely, so after Bxg5 Nxg5 Rg8 f4 you were shuffling your knight to safety instead of attacking, handing back 1.4 pawns of a near-winning position. Bh4 sidesteps the trade entirely — the bishop slides to safety without being exchanged, and after Rg8 Nbd2 Bh3 Bg3 Bg4 you're still pushing forward with everything intact. When a piece is attacked, look first for moves that keep it working, not just moves that develop something else.

drills.title: vs bbaldy87 (312) — Owens Defense
drills.coachNote: White's queen on f3 sits behind its own e4 pawn, and once that pawn pushes to e5 the diagonal opens all the way to your pawn on b7 and rook on a8. Nf6 puts your knight right in that pawn's path — e5 attacks it immediately, and in the game it got left there and lost outright to exf6, a brutal 3.3 pawn swing for one careless move. Nc6 instead develops a piece that's nowhere near that diagonal, and after Nh3 h6 c3 e5 Bc4 you're simply playing a normal, level game. When White plays an odd early queen move like Qf3, ask what it's pointing at before developing on autopilot.

drills.coachNote: White's king never castled and is still on e1, sitting on the very diagonal your bishop on c2 occupies — give White a free move and he starts untangling with a3, then kicks your queen with f4. That's what happened after Qe5: White consolidated calmly, Nc6 held, and f4 booted your queen back to e4, handing back 1.5 pawns even though you were still completely winning. Bb4+ instead cashes in on that diagonal right away — it forces Nc3 to block, and after Bxc3+ bxc3 Qxc3+ Kf2 you've wrecked White's pawns and keep grabbing material with check after check. drills.coachNote: Black's knight on c6 is the only piece standing between your d-pawn and a fork — remove it and d4-d5 hits both the queen on d6 and the bishop on e6 at once. Nxc6 instead clears the blocker first: after Qxc6 d5 Qe8 dxe6 Rd8, the fork lands exactly as planned and you come out a clean piece ahead instead of scrambling for tricks. drills.coachNote: White's rook on b6 is eyeing b8 — a back-rank check that only works if your king has drifted too far away to deal with it. Stepping to d8 puts your king just out of range: White plays Rb8+ safely, you're forced into the ugly Nc8 block, and c6 rolls forward with everything tangled on the back rank — already down 2.7, you crash into a near-lost position. Kc8 keeps the king one square closer instead, so if White tries Rb8+ you simply answer Kxb8; you still have to deal with c6, Bc4, and losing the knight to dxe7, but your king stays active enough to hold. Qg2# instead sends the queen from c6 straight down the diagonal with check; the king can't capture since your rook on f2 guards that square, and every other flight square is covered — mate on the spot.
